regions.label: Head
regions.anatomy: Skull, jaw, face. Cranks lever the head to load the cervical spine; chokes are set up by head position (chin strap, cross-face).

regions.label: Neck
regions.anatomy: Cervical spine (C1–C7), carotid arteries and jugular veins (blood chokes), trachea (air chokes).

regions.label: Shoulder
regions.anatomy: Glenohumeral joint, rotator cuff, anterior capsule. Rotational locks (kimura, americana, omoplata) attack it.

regions.label: Upper arm
regions.anatomy: Humerus, biceps brachii and brachialis — the bicep slicer compresses these against a fulcrum.

regions.label: Elbow
regions.anatomy: Humeroulnar joint, ulnar collateral ligament, anterior capsule. Hyperextension locks (armbar) attack it.

regions.label: Forearm
regions.anatomy: Radius/ulna, pronation–supination. Common grip point for kimura, americana and wrist locks.

regions.label: Wrist
regions.anatomy: Radiocarpal joint and carpal ligaments. Wrist locks flex, extend or rotate it past range.

regions.label: Hand
regions.anatomy: Carpals/metacarpals and fingers. Grip-fighting target; finger locks are illegal in IBJJF.

regions.label: Chest
regions.anatomy: Thoracic spine, rib cage, sternum. Chest-to-chest pressure and the mount/side-control pins load it.

regions.label: Abdomen / spine
regions.anatomy: Lumbar spine, abdominal wall. Spinal locks (twister) and knee-on-belly pressure target it.

regions.label: Hips
regions.anatomy: Pelvis, hip joints, adductors/groin. Hip control is the heart of pins and guard; the banana split attacks the adductors.

regions.label: Thigh
regions.anatomy: Femur, quadriceps, hamstrings. Leg-entanglement controls (inside position, knee line) live here.

regions.label: Knee
regions.anatomy: Tibiofemoral joint; ACL/PCL, MCL/LCL, menisci. Heel hooks rotate it; kneebars hyperextend it.

regions.label: Shin / calf
regions.anatomy: Tibia/fibula, gastrocnemius and soleus. Calf slicers compress the calf against a fulcrum.

regions.label: Ankle
regions.anatomy: Talocrural and subtalar joints, Achilles tendon. Straight ankle locks and toe holds attack it.

regions.label: Foot
regions.anatomy: Tarsals, metatarsals, toes. The grip point for toe holds and heel hooks.

techniques.name: 50/50 guard (and 80/20) control

structures: knee line of both players' inside legs
primary_target.mechanism: Both players' inside legs are intertwined with feet crossed and knees up – a closed-circuit entanglement controlling the opponent's hip and knee that gives each player identical access to the inside (reverse) heel hook, straight ankle lock and toe hold. Dropping the inside knee toward the mat and triangling (80/20) hides your own knee line so only you keep the heel hook.

secondary_targets.mechanism: In gi the position is mostly used for sweeps and back takes; the IBJJF penalises lapel/belt grips held here without progression (6.2.1 F) and awards no advantages for sweeps starting and ending in 50/50 (5.7.5).

positions.note: Reached in scrambles or by switching the leg over from outside ashi (Kesting & Biernacki position 4–5).

ibjjf.note: Legal at all belts; white–purple may only finish the straight ankle lock here and turning inside while the opponent stands on the guard foot is a trapped-foot reap (p. 33).

techniques.summary: Symmetrical leg entanglement – whatever you can do they can do – unless you hide your inside knee (80/20) and keep the heel hook for yourself.

techniques.name: Americana

structures: anterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament
primary_target.mechanism: Forced external rotation of the humerus with the shoulder abducted ~90 deg and the elbow flexed ~90 deg: the wrist is pinned to the mat and the elbow is lifted/dragged toward the hip ('paintbrush'), loading the anterior capsule and anterior IGHL - the apprehension position

secondary_targets.mechanism: Elbow is flexed and used as the lever; some torque reaches the elbow if the wrist slides

techniques.name: Aoki lock

structures: knee rotational restraints (medial side per Evolve; posterolateral per the inside-heel-hook anatomy)
primary_target.mechanism: From a straight-ashi/ankle-lock type hold where the heel is hidden, the elbow goes under the foot and an RNC-style grip is taken on the attacker's own shoulders; the foot is turned outward and the heel inward so the ankle is held in outward rotation, then a linear (ankle) and rotational (knee) force is applied – 'essentially an inside heel hook twisting the leg outward' (Kesting).

secondary_targets.mechanism: Rotational finish transfers torque to the knee like an inverted heel hook (Evolve).
Kesting warns of broken ankle bones.

techniques.name: Arm-in guillotine

primary_target.mechanism: One of the opponent's arms is trapped inside the headlock; the forearm compresses one carotid/trachea while the opponent's own trapped shoulder closes the other side, similar to an arm triangle mechanism

secondary_targets.mechanism: Opponent's own shoulder is driven into the neck

positions.note: Arises when the opponent's arm is inside the headlock after a sprawl
Finish from guard with elbows tight and hips driven in
Common when the passer's head drops low

ibjjf.note: Covered by rows 5 (frontal guillotine) and 8 (arm triangle): illegal under 16 only.

techniques.summary: A guillotine where the opponent's arm is trapped inside the choke; relies on the opponent's own shoulder to close the far side of the neck.
techniques.notes: Mechanism description taken from coaching sources, not textbooks.

techniques.name: Armbar from back control

primary_target.mechanism: Elbow hyperextension: from the back the attacker traps the arm (often with a kimura or wrist grip), swings a leg over the head and falls to the side to extend the elbow over the hips

positions.note: When the opponent defends the choke with the hands, trap the top arm and rotate to the armbar; Kesting lists armbars from 'kimura control from the back'
See armbar_crucifix

techniques.summary: A choke-defence counter from the back: control the arm, throw the leg over the head and extend the elbow.
techniques.notes: Garcia 2011 covers finishing from the back but exact pages were not verified.

techniques.name: Armbar from closed guard

primary_target.mechanism: Elbow hyperextension: the attacker's hips act as the fulcrum below the elbow while the wrist is pulled to the chest; forearm kept neutral/thumb-up so the olecranon locks in the fossa and the medial elbow complex (UCL, flexor origin, anterior capsule) is loaded in tension

secondary_targets.mechanism: Arm is pulled across and up; knees pinch the upper arm, limiting rotation

positions.note: Break posture, control the wrist/sleeve, angle the hips, leg over the head, squeeze knees and lift hips
Same finish from open guard once an arm is isolated

ibjjf.note: Not on the IBJJF prohibited-techniques table (Rules Book v6.1 p. 29); legal in every division including kids

techniques.summary: The classic cross armlock from the guard: pull the arm across your centreline, swing a leg over the head, pinch the knees and raise the hips to hyperextend the elbow.
techniques.notes: Which structure fails first is debated: the 2017 MRI case series found UCL and common flexor tendon injury; a cadaver study reported second-hand (Sherdog) found anterior capsule rupture first.

techniques.name: Armbar from mount / S-mount / technical mount

primary_target.mechanism: Elbow hyperextension over the attacker's hips/pelvis with the wrist pinned to the chest and the forearm neutral; knees squeezed to immobilise the humerus

positions.note: Isolate one arm (often when the opponent pushes the chest), step to S-mount, swing the leg over the head and sit back
The S-mount pins the arm against the attacker's thigh and blocks the head with the knee before the finish
Technical mount gives direct access to the far/top arm for the armbar
Near-arm armbar when the opponent pushes the knee

techniques.summary: From mount the attacker climbs to S-mount, traps the arm against the thigh, swings the leg over the head and sits back for the hyperextension.

techniques.name: Armbar from side control (far-arm / spinning armbar)

primary_target.mechanism: Elbow hyperextension: the far arm is isolated under the attacker's armpit or across the chest, the attacker steps/spins over the head and extends the elbow over the hips or the thigh

positions.note: Trap the far arm (e.g., when the opponent pushes on the hip/face), step over the head and spin to the armbar; Theory & Technique lists 'Arm bar from across-side position'
Arm isolated while circling to north-south
Spinning armbar on the far arm

techniques.summary: Top-side armlock: isolate the far arm, step over the head and fall back into the cross armlock.

sources.locator: entry 'Arm bar from across-side position' (LibraryThing contents listing)

techniques.name: Armbar from spider guard

primary_target.mechanism: Elbow hyperextension: the sleeve grip pulls the arm while the foot on the biceps pushes the upper arm, pre-extending the elbow; the attacker angles the hips and throws the leg over the head to finish

positions.note: Pull the sleeve, push the biceps with the foot, move the other foot to the hip, swing the leg over the head (gi)
Lasso isolates the arm for the same finish

ibjjf.note: Spider/lasso grips require the gi sleeve; no-gi equivalents use wrist control

techniques.summary: Gi-specific armbar: the sleeve-and-foot-on-biceps tension already straightens the arm, so the attacker only has to angle and swing the leg over the head.

techniques.name: Armbar from the crucifix (leg-trapped arm)

primary_target.mechanism: Elbow hyperextension using the legs: the arm trapped between the attacker's thighs is straightened and the attacker bridges the hips forward against the elbow while the legs are triangled to remove slack

positions.note: Bottom-leg triangle version, or top-leg triangle after the opponent turns the arm (hitchhiker)

techniques.summary: With one arm captured between the legs in the crucifix, the attacker extends the elbow with a hip bridge instead of the hands.

techniques.name: Ashi garami / single-leg X control

structures: knee line (femoral condyles pinched between the attacker's thighs)
primary_target.mechanism: Outside heel on the opponent's hip, inside leg hooks under/around the thigh, knees pinched and heels retracted so the trapped knee stays inside the attacker's knee line; initially both legs are controlled ('double trouble') to deny base. Open-circuit (ankles not crossed) – the 'jab' of leg locks.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Foot on the hip controls distance and prevents the opponent from following into a pass.
Foot clamped in the armpit for the straight ankle lock or outside heel hook.

positions.note: Primary; also attacks SLX sweeps.
Entries from most bottom guards and 'almost all top open-guard positions' (Kesting & Biernacki); upgrades to cross ashi, outside ashi, inside ashi or the 411.

ibjjf.note: Legal position; only the straight ankle lock may be finished below brown, and the foot must not cross the midline (reap).

techniques.summary: Both legs wrap one of theirs with your foot on their hip and knees pinched – the gateway position for the straight ankle lock and the outside heel hook.

techniques.name: Backside 50/50 heel hook

primary_target.mechanism: An ashi garami in which the attacker's hips face AWAY from the opponent and the outside hip sits on the trapped leg; inside leg hooks behind the knee, outside leg crosses the thigh, knees pinch. The foot is pulled to the chest with toes on the attacker's centreline and the body rotated – an inside-heel-hook (external tibial rotation) finish with the opponent unable to turn in.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Attacker's hip sits low on the knee, pinning the hip line so the opponent cannot 'boot-scoot' or spin to relieve pressure.

positions.note: Entered by turning away from a normal 50/50 or from a failed saddle / rolling back take; transitions back to 50/50.
Backside entries from 50/50 are a listed route into the saddle (Digitsu).

ibjjf.note: Heel hook rules apply (row 17): Adult brown/black no-gi only; the leg configuration is also a reap in gi.

techniques.summary: A 50/50 played with your back to the opponent: hips heavy on their knee, foot hugged to the chest, finished with an inside heel hook they cannot turn away from.

sources.locator: lists backside 50-50 as a key position

techniques.notes: Single detailed source for the configuration; popularisation (often credited to Lachlan Giles / Craig Jones) not verified.

techniques.name: Banana split

structures: hip adductor group (adductor longus/brevis/magnus, gracilis, pectineus)
primary_target.mechanism: One leg is anchored with a lockdown/leg lace and driven away while the other leg is pulled toward the attacker's chest (gable or S-grip behind the knee or on the ankle); squeezing the knees together and extending the hips forces the two legs apart into extreme hip abduction – a splits the opponent cannot resist.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Muscle strain/tear can precede the tap in flexible opponents.

positions.note: The truck (lockdown from twister side control / back-control variant) is the standard position; electric chair and quarter guard are listed too (Digitsu).
Remove the top hook, lockdown the near leg, grab the far leg and fall back (Evolve).
Bottom hook in, foot over the ankle, grab the feet and fall back; or finish with a calf crush (Evolve).

ibjjf.note: 'Submission techniques stretching legs apart' (row 1) is banned ONLY for 4–12-year-olds – legal for all adult belts.

techniques.summary: From the truck, pin one leg with a lockdown and pull the other to your chest: the opponent is forced into the splits and taps to the groin and hamstrings.
techniques.notes: Specific adductor muscles are the author's anatomical gloss; sources say 'groin and hamstrings'. Some sources also classify it loosely as a 'spinal lock'; the IBJJF treats leg-splitting as its own class.

techniques.name: Baratoplata

primary_target.mechanism: Forced internal rotation: the opponent's elbow is clamped between the attacker's thighs (triangle-like), the attacker threads an arm through the bent arm (reverse-kimura frame seated in the elbow crook) and pushes the wrist outward and upward while turning the torso toward the trapped shoulder

positions.note: Reverse-kimura grip, wrist pinned to the belly, elbow trapped by the thighs, angle the hips
From a defended mounted armbar: thread the arm through the elbow and lock the figure-four
Against an extended frame, step over the head
From armbar/triangle control

ibjjf.note: A shoulder lock, not on the prohibited table; Caio Terra won the 2015 IBJJF No-Gi Worlds final with it

techniques.summary: Rafael 'Barata' Freitas' shoulder lock: elbow pinned between the thighs, your arm threaded through the crook, wrist pushed out and up.
techniques.notes: Sources disagree on the precise direction of the finishing torque (rotate torso vs push arm away); Freitas originally developed it as a bicep slicer and converted it to a shoulder lock for rules compliance.

techniques.name: Baseball bat choke

primary_target.mechanism: Stacked collar grips (one palm up, one palm down like holding a bat); the attacker spins toward north-south, driving chest weight so the forearms and collar close across both carotids and the windpipe

positions.note: Classic setup: grips set from KOB, then spin to north-south
From kesa-gatame style control
Bottom variant (Magid Hage)

ibjjf.note: Gi only; legal in all divisions.

techniques.summary: Stacked bat-style collar grips finished by spinning to north-south; famous late-tap choke.
techniques.notes: Single instructional source; textbook locator not found.

techniques.name: Bicep slicer

structures: biceps brachii and brachialis muscle bellies
primary_target.mechanism: Compression: a bony fulcrum (shin, forearm/radius, or wrist) is wedged deep into the antecubital fossa and the forearm is forcibly flexed over it, crushing the biceps/brachialis and distal biceps tendon against the humerus

secondary_targets.mechanism: The fulcrum inside the bent elbow distracts/separates the joint (why judo treats it as an armlock)

positions.note: Thread the arm inside the elbow, control the wrist, open the guard and fold the arm over your forearm
Shin across the elbow crease provides the fulcrum
Shin-in-elbow slicers appear in 10th Planet material
After a defended mounted armbar: leg over the forearm, lock a triangle and squeeze
From a defended kimura, go deeper into the figure-four with the forearm as the blade
Pin the near arm with the inside leg and drive the hips

ibjjf.note: IBJJF Rules Book v6.1 p. 29 table row 12: prohibited for all kids/juvenile divisions and for adult white, blue and purple belts; permitted for adult brown and black belts (gi and no-gi)

techniques.summary: Fold the opponent's arm over your shin or forearm wedged in the crook of the elbow and squeeze the biceps against the bone.
techniques.notes: Legality verified against the rendered IBJJF table (2026-10-11). Rubber guard position cited to Bravo without a page locator.

techniques.name: Boston crab

structures: lumbar spine (facet joints, anterior longitudinal ligament)
primary_target.mechanism: Opponent face-down; attacker holds both legs under the arms and sits back on the lumbar region, forcing lumbar hyperextension

secondary_targets.mechanism: Hip hyperextension

positions.note: Attacker standing/sitting over a prone opponent; arises from leg-entanglement scrambles

ibjjf.note: Row 22 'Spinal lock without choke': illegal in every division.

techniques.summary: Pro-wrestling-derived lumbar hyperextension lock; a pure spinal lock and illegal under IBJJF rules.
techniques.notes: Rare in BJJ; included for completeness of spinal locks.

techniques.name: Bow and arrow choke

primary_target.mechanism: Deep collar grip across the neck from the back while the other hand controls the far pant leg; the attacker extends the body like drawing a bow so the collar cuts across both carotids with full-body leverage

secondary_targets.mechanism: Leg is pulled to stretch the opponent and prevent them turning

positions.note: The highest-percentage gi finish from the back; Ribeiro teaches it as the back's main collar attack
From the clock-choke setup, pull the leg and roll

ibjjf.note: Gi only; legal in all divisions.

techniques.summary: Back-control collar choke finished by gripping the far leg and extending the body like a bow; the most common gi choke in modern competition.

techniques.name: Buggy choke

primary_target.mechanism: From bottom side control the defender throws the far leg over the top player's head/neck and locks the same-side arm under the knee (figure-four of arm and leg); the head and one arm are trapped so the thigh and the opponent's shoulder compress both carotids, as in a triangle

positions.note: Attacks the top player's head when they stay chest-to-chest with the far arm exposed
Also hit from bottom of turtle/kesa gatame

ibjjf.note: Not in the illegal-moves table; a pure strangle, so legal in all adult divisions. Mostly a no-gi competition technique.

techniques.summary: Bottom-side-control strangle: leg over the opponent's head, arm locked under the leg, squeeze.
techniques.notes: Sources differ on the exact arm/leg path; no textbook treatment (it is a 2010s-era technique).

techniques.name: Calf slicer

structures: popliteal fossa neurovascular bundle (tibial nerve, popliteal vessels)
primary_target.mechanism: A rigid wedge (attacker's shin or forearm) is placed deep behind the knee and the opponent's heel is pulled toward the buttock; forced knee flexion over the fulcrum compresses the calf musculature and posterior knee against the wedge, with hip extension adding force.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Continued pressure hyperflexes and levers the joint open (the 'knee separator'); Wikipedia and Digitsu note potential joint separation / ACL-PCL stress.

positions.note: Truck (10th Planet back-control leg entanglement): lockdown on one leg while the other is pulled – the classic entry (Bravo vs Royler, Metamoris III).
Back-step over the entangled leg from top half guard / DLR with the shin already behind the knee.
Lockdown switched to a figure-four from bottom half guard.
Hook the near leg from behind a turtled opponent with the shin on the calf.
Sit down on the foot with the forearm behind the knee (LowKick).
Listed entry; also as a follow-up to a failed kneebar (Digitsu).

ibjjf.note: Row 13: brown/black only, gi and no-gi.

techniques.summary: A compression lock, not a joint lock: your shin or forearm behind the knee becomes a blade the calf is folded over when you pull the heel to the buttock.
techniques.notes: Specific muscles (gastrocnemius/soleus) are the author's anatomical gloss – sources say 'calf muscle'. Not covered in the Hasegawa review.

techniques.name: Can opener
aliases: Neck crank from inside the guard

structures: cervical spine (C-spine facet joints, posterior ligaments)
primary_target.mechanism: From inside the closed guard the top player clasps both hands behind the opponent's head and pulls it into forced forward flexion toward the chest while driving the hips forward

positions.note: Historically used to open the guard; now a pure crank

ibjjf.note: Row 22 'Spinal lock without choke': illegal in every division (kids through adult brown/black no-gi).

techniques.summary: Pulling the opponent's head forward from inside their guard; a cervical flexion crank banned in IBJJF at every level.

techniques.name: Chest-to-chest side control pressure

primary_target.mechanism: Attacker's chest is driven across the opponent's chest with hips low and weight off the knees, compressing the ribcage and limiting breathing; combined with cross-face and underhook to immobilise the shoulders

secondary_targets.mechanism: Cross-face often added
Underhook pins the far shoulder

positions.note: Ribeiro's side-control survival chapter is built around escaping this pressure
Pressure shifts to the chest/face
Low mount chest pressure

ibjjf.note: Legal; passing to side control scores 3 points (guard pass), side control itself scores none.

techniques.summary: Heavy chest-on-chest pin from side control; the baseline control every escape chapter begins with.

sources.locator: Ch. 8 Winning From the Top Position

techniques.name: Chin strap

primary_target.mechanism: Hand cups the chin from the front headlock (or from side control) so the head cannot turn or lift; the elbow is kept tight to block posture, setting up guillotines, D'Arce and back takes

secondary_targets.mechanism: Head held in flexion

positions.note: First grip of Danaher's front headlock system
Chin strap sets up head-and-arm chokes and prevents turning in
After a snap-down

ibjjf.note: Legal; hand must not grip the throat/windpipe (6.2.3-I).

techniques.summary: Hand under the chin controlling the head from the front headlock; the entry to guillotine family attacks.

techniques.name: Clock choke

primary_target.mechanism: Against a turtled opponent the attacker takes a deep collar grip across the neck, drops chest weight on the upper back and walks the feet around the head like a clock hand; the collar and the attacker's weight compress the carotids

positions.note: Rear knee blocks the gap between opponent's elbow and knee; walk toward the head

ibjjf.note: Gi only; legal in all divisions.

techniques.summary: Turtle-position lapel choke finished by walking around the opponent's head with body weight on the collar grip.

techniques.name: Closed-guard rib/kidney compression

primary_target.mechanism: Bottom player locks the ankles and squeezes the knees/thighs around the torso, compressing the lower ribs and flank

secondary_targets.mechanism: Rib compression

positions.note: Squeezing the legs as a submission (do-jime in judo)

ibjjf.note: Row 9 'Lock inside the closed guard with legs compressing kidneys or ribs': illegal for 4-12, 13-15, 16-17 and adult white belts; legal from blue belt (adult) in gi and no-gi.

techniques.summary: Squeezing the opponent's ribs with the closed guard; banned in judo and for IBJJF white belts.
techniques.notes: Mechanism is straightforward; included because it is the only torso-compression entry in the IBJJF table.

techniques.name: Collar tie

primary_target.mechanism: Hand cups the back of the neck with the forearm on the chest; pulling down forces the opponent's head and posture forward, enabling snap-downs, duck-unders and shots

secondary_targets.mechanism: Head pulled down

positions.note: Wrestling clinch control; in the gi, the collar grip plays the same role

ibjjf.note: Legal.

techniques.summary: Hand behind the neck in the standing clinch to break posture and control the head.

techniques.name: Cross ashi / outside ashi control

primary_target.mechanism: The trapped leg is switched across the attacker's body (cross ashi) or the inside leg steps over it and the ankles cross with the outside foot on top (outside ashi, closed circuit). Hips are pulled close to the opponent, the top knee flares as a frame, and the attacker constantly bridges ('bridge wedge') so the knee is immobilised and the opponent cannot pull the leg out.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Hip is wedged so the opponent cannot turn into the rotation; from cross ashi the leg-drag pass is also available.

positions.note: Attacks: outside heel hook, 'cross ankle lock', toe hold, Z-lock; transition to 50/50 or the 411 (Kesting & Biernacki positions 2–3).
Abandoning cross ashi flows straight into a leg drag pass.

ibjjf.note: Position legal provided the foot does not cross the midline / the knee is not pressured from outside-in with the foot trapped (reap, row 19).

techniques.summary: Upgrade from standard ashi: cross the ankles over the trapped leg, hips in, knee flared, always bridging – better control and a stronger heel hook.

sources.locator: cross ashi / outside ashi as safe inside positions

techniques.notes: Naming is inconsistent across schools: Digitsu uses 'cross ashi garami' for the saddle; Kesting/Biernacki use it for the open-circuit topside ashi. This entry follows Kesting/Biernacki.

techniques.name: Cross collar choke

primary_target.mechanism: Both hands grip deep in opposite collars so the forearms cross in an X across the neck; pulling the elbows down/in drives the radial edges of the forearms and the collar into both carotids

positions.note: Roger Gracie's signature; first grip deep behind the neck, drop the head
The first submission taught in most gi curricula
Grips set while the opponent frames
Top half guard variant

ibjjf.note: Gi only (requires collars). Legal in all divisions. 6.2.2-S: using an untied belt to assist a choke is a penalty.

techniques.summary: Classic gi strangle: cross grips on the collars, pull the elbows to the ribs to compress the carotids with the collar and forearms.

techniques.name: Cross-face

primary_target.mechanism: Attacker's forearm or shoulder is driven across the opponent's jaw/face, turning the head away from the attacker; where the head goes the spine follows, so hip movement and bridging are shut down

secondary_targets.mechanism: Forced rotation/lateral flexion

positions.note: The standard side-control head control (Ribeiro)
Cross-face + underhook is the core top half-guard control
Low mount cross-face
Wrestling-style cross-face to break down the turtle

ibjjf.note: Legal; must not become a neck crank (row 22) or hand pressure on the windpipe (6.2.3-I).

techniques.summary: Forearm/shoulder across the face turns the opponent's head away, killing their ability to turn in or bridge.

sources.locator: Survival / Guard passing chapters (side control pressure)

techniques.name: Crucifix (arm trapped between the legs)

structures: upper arm / elbow (clamped between the attacker's thighs)
far arm (controlled by the attacker's arms/seatbelt)
primary_target.mechanism: One of the opponent's arms is isolated between the attacker's thighs (often triangled) while the other is controlled with the hands, spreading the arms like a cross; the trapped arm can be armbarred, keylocked or rotated with the legs, and the free hands attack the neck

secondary_targets.mechanism: Chokes become available with both of the opponent's arms occupied

positions.note: Primary position
Entered from side-ride on turtle or from an arm drag; lock the thighs on the arm and lift with the outside leg

ibjjf.note: Control is legal; bicep-slicer finishes from here are brown-belt-only

techniques.summary: Both of the opponent's arms are tied up - one by your legs, one by your arms - so that nothing can defend the chokes and leg-armlocks that follow.

techniques.name: Crucifix choke

primary_target.mechanism: From the back-control crucifix (one of the opponent's arms trapped between the attacker's legs, the other controlled by the attacker's arm) the free arm wraps the neck, or feeds a lapel, and the attacker extends to strangle

positions.note: Reached from the turtle / failed single leg; Kesting's 'traditional crucifix'
Entry position

ibjjf.note: Choke from the crucifix is legal at all levels (only the neck-crank 'cattle catch' is prohibited under row 22).

techniques.summary: Strangle from the crucifix back-control position with both of the opponent's arms trapped.

techniques.name: Crucifix control

primary_target.mechanism: From the back/turtle, one of the opponent's arms is trapped between the attacker's legs and the other by the attacker's arm, leaving both arms unable to defend the neck

secondary_targets.mechanism: Neck is defenceless

positions.note: Reached from turtle, failed single leg or fireman's carry
Entry

ibjjf.note: Position is legal at all levels; only the neck-crank finish is prohibited.

techniques.summary: Back-side control with the opponent's arms spread by legs and arm; sets up collar and arm chokes.

techniques.name: Crucifix neck crank

primary_target.mechanism: Opponent's arms are held out (one between the attacker's legs, one under the arm) while the attacker, facing away, sits back and forces the head into flexion/extension against the trapped shoulders

secondary_targets.mechanism: Arms are spread to immobilise the shoulder girdle

positions.note: The 'other' crucifix (Kesting); legal only in no-gi submission wrestling / MMA

ibjjf.note: Row 22 'Spinal lock without choke': illegal in every division. ADCC also forbids the crucifix neck crank.

techniques.summary: Catch-wrestling crucifix crank with both arms spread; illegal in BJJ competition.

techniques.name: D'Arce choke

primary_target.mechanism: Arm-triangle variant: choking arm threads under the opponent's near arm, across the front of the neck and on top of the far arm, gripping own biceps; forearm compresses one carotid and the trapped shoulder the other

secondary_targets.mechanism: Pinned into the neck by the attacker's chest

positions.note: From sprawl/turtle when the opponent's arm is inside
Classic entry when the bottom player's underhook arm is exposed
When opponent turns in with the arm extended
Thread under the near arm from the side

ibjjf.note: Treated as an arm triangle (row 8): illegal under 16 only.

techniques.summary: Arm-in choke threaded under the near arm and over the far arm; named for Joe D'Arce, popularised in no-gi.

techniques.name: Electric chair

primary_target.mechanism: From the dogfight reached via the lockdown, the underhook arm threads deep under the opponent's far thigh and the hands clasp; the attacker falls to that shoulder, pulls the far leg across the chest and extends the hips/arches the back so the legs are split apart. Popularised by Eddie Bravo / 10th Planet (used on Royler Gracie at Metamoris III).

secondary_targets.mechanism: Stretch injury before the tap in flexible people.

positions.note: Lockdown half guard → whip-up → dogfight → electric chair; doubles as a sweep entry; follow-ups are twister, banana split and vaporizer (Digitsu).
Dogfight position.

ibjjf.note: Leg-splitting submissions (row 1) are banned only for 4–12; legal for all adult belts.

techniques.summary: From the lockdown dogfight, thread an arm under the far thigh, fall to the shoulder and arch – a sweep that becomes a groin stretch if they do not roll.
techniques.notes: Eddie Bravo's 'Mastering the Rubber Guard' (2006) covers the lockdown/electric chair system but no page locator was found.

techniques.name: Estima lock

primary_target.mechanism: The opponent's foot is pushing on the attacker's hip/abdomen; the attacker wraps one forearm under the Achilles and heel (rear-naked-choke style), clasps the other hand over the top of the foot and pins the dorsum against the belly with the toes pointing inward, then rotates the torso toward the foot and drives the hips forward – forcing plantarflexion + inversion, a toe-hold-type torque.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Residual torque passes to the knee once the foot is at end range, as with any twisting foot lock.

positions.note: Counter to a foot on the hip/abdomen while knee-cutting or pressure passing (Braulio Estima's demonstration).
Against the RDLR/foot-on-hip frame.
Counter to the lasso hook (Digitsu).
Also from single-leg X and X-guard bottom (Digitsu).
Torreando passing and scrambles when the opponent pushes off with a foot.

ibjjf.note: Not named in the rulebook; its twisting mechanics place it in the toe-hold class (row 15) – brown/black. Victor Estima won the 2011 IBJJF No-Gi Worlds with it.

techniques.summary: Catch a foot that is pushing on your hip, wrap the heel RNC-style, pin the top of the foot to your belly and turn – a toe hold without a figure-four.
techniques.notes: IBJJF classification inferred from mechanics, not stated in the rulebook.

techniques.name: Ezekiel choke

primary_target.mechanism: One arm wraps behind the head and grips inside the other sleeve; the free forearm/fist passes across the front of the neck and the two arms scissor, compressing carotids and (depending on placement) the trachea

positions.note: Standard application; Ribeiro covers it in mount submissions
Legal and effective from inside guard
Top half guard
Occasional

techniques.summary: Sleeve-gripping forearm scissor choke named after judoka Ezequiel Paraguassu; works from mount or even from inside the guard.

techniques.name: Finger lock / small-joint manipulation

primary_target.mechanism: Hyperextension (or lateral deviation) of one or more fingers against the volar plate and collateral ligaments

positions.note: Any grip-fighting situation; shown here only so the hand region surfaces the rule

ibjjf.note: IBJJF Rules Book v6.1 p. 29 table row 24 'Bending fingers backwards' is prohibited in every division, gi and no-gi. Grabbing fewer than four fingers to break a grip is also restricted (item 6.2.2 H concerns fingers inside the sleeve/pant opening)

techniques.summary: Bending fingers back is banned at all belts under IBJJF rules; wrist locks on the whole hand are legal from blue belt.

sources.locator: note on combining hyperextending wristlocks with fingerlocks

techniques.notes: Included as a legality marker rather than a taught technique.

techniques.name: Flying armbar

primary_target.mechanism: Elbow hyperextension: from standing the attacker controls the arm (and collar/neck in no-gi), places a shin on the opponent's hip/midsection, jumps and swings the other leg over the head, landing in the cross armlock

positions.note: Usually against a collar tie or a stiff arm; high risk if the opponent does not support the weight

ibjjf.note: The armbar itself is legal, but IBJJF Rules Book v6.1 item 6.2.2 W penalises jumping to closed guard 'including any and all attacks initiated by jumping guard, such as ... Flying Triangles and Flying Armbars' in all under-15 divisions and all white-belt age groups

techniques.summary: A standing jump into the cross armlock; spectacular but risky, and effectively banned for white belts and under-15s under IBJJF rules.

techniques.name: Front headlock

primary_target.mechanism: Attacker wraps the opponent's head and one arm from the front after a sprawl or snap-down, chest weight on the back of the neck forcing flexion; controls the head to prevent shots and set up guillotine, anaconda, D'Arce and back takes

secondary_targets.mechanism: Arm controlled at the elbow/triceps

positions.note: The position itself
Against turtle
After sprawling on a shot

ibjjf.note: Legal control; pulling the head down with no choke can be ruled a spinal lock (row 22) if applied as a submission.

techniques.summary: Head-and-arm control from the front, hub of the guillotine/D'Arce/anaconda system.

techniques.name: Gift wrap

structures: humerus / shoulder (arm folded across the face)
primary_target.mechanism: One of the opponent's arms is folded across their own face/neck and pinned: in no-gi the attacker grips the wrist deep behind the head from the opposite side; in gi the opponent's own lapel is fed over the arm; chest pressure keeps them flat

secondary_targets.mechanism: The trapped forearm lies across the face, limiting head movement

structures: opponent's own arm wrapped across the neck
secondary_targets.mechanism: The opponent's arm is pulled across their own throat and pinned there with a 2-on-1 / kimura-style grip from behind the head; the trapped arm immobilises the head and shoulders and exposes the back
Arm wrapped across the body
Wrist gripped behind the neck

positions.note: From mount/technical mount; leads to back take, armbar or chokes
Feed the near arm across the face and pin it
Standard follow-up from the gift wrap
Seen in top half guard and 3/4 mount

ibjjf.note: Control only; pressing the forearm into the face is legal but hands blocking nose/mouth airflow is a severe foul (6.2.3 J)

techniques.summary: Fold the opponent's arm across their own face and hold the wrist from the other side; a Rickson-era control leading to the back, crucifix or armbar.
techniques.notes: Attribution to Rickson Gracie is from secondary blogs, not verified in a textbook. Merged with the torso-control entry from the neck/torso research set.

techniques.name: Gogoplata

primary_target.mechanism: From rubber guard / omoplata setup the shin or instep is placed across the front of the throat; pulling the head down onto the shin compresses the windpipe and carotids

secondary_targets.mechanism: Hands pull the head down onto the shin

positions.note: Bravo's rubber guard finish; locoplata uses the free foot to push the choking foot
From a high guard / omoplata position
Mounted gogoplata variant

ibjjf.note: Not listed in the 6.2.3-M table; legal in all adult divisions. 6.2.2-R (foot in the lapel behind the neck) is a separate penalty in the gi.

techniques.summary: Shin-across-the-throat choke from the rubber guard, popularised by Eddie Bravo and Nick Diaz.
techniques.notes: Primarily tracheal in most descriptions; legality inferred from absence in the official table and fan tables that mark it legal.

techniques.name: Grapevine hooks (mount)

primary_target.mechanism: From mount the top player loops each leg over and under the opponent's legs, crossing at the ankle or calf so the two legs interlock; the hooks anchor the opponent's legs to the mat and the top player drives the hips forward with core engaged, making bridging and shrimping far harder.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Stretching the hooks out spreads and extends the hips; a leg-lock variant from the grapevine is described (bjjee) but not an IBJJF-named technique.
Hooks are set at ankle or calf.

positions.note: Low mount control; loosen the grapevine when attacking the americana in case of a bridge (Evolve). Bottom escape: straighten and kick the trapped leg, turn to half guard.

techniques.summary: Mount with your legs woven around theirs: anchors their legs so they cannot bridge or shrimp, at the cost of some mobility.
techniques.notes: Hip-stretch effect is practitioner knowledge, not stated by the sources.

techniques.name: Guillotine choke

primary_target.mechanism: Forearm/wrist blade is drawn up and across the front of the neck while the attacker's chest and the opponent's own shoulder close the other side; the high-elbow version angles the forearm onto the carotids (blood choke), the standard version compresses the trachea as well (air + blood)

secondary_targets.mechanism: Head is pulled down into forward flexion by the front headlock before the squeeze

positions.note: From a sprawl / snap-down; Danaher's front headlock system treats it as the primary finish
Pull guard with the head trapped; squeeze while legs control posture
Counter to a low shot or a head-down clinch
Marcelotine / arm-in entries when opponent's head drops

ibjjf.note: Row 5 'Frontal guillotine choke' is illegal for 4-12 and 13-15 y.o. only; legal from 16 y.o./white belt in gi and no-gi. Row 2 'Choke with spinal lock' (crank-heavy guillotines) is legal from 16 y.o. too.

techniques.summary: Front headlock choke: wrap the neck from the front, grip your own hand or biceps, and squeeze upward while controlling the opponent's posture. Marcelo Garcia and Danaher popularised the high-elbow variant.
techniques.notes: Blood vs air split depends on forearm placement; coaching sources agree the high-elbow version is primarily carotid and the low 'wrist in the throat' version is primarily tracheal.

techniques.name: Half guard leg trap with underhook

structures: opponent's trapped thigh, knee and shin (between the bottom player's legs)
primary_target.mechanism: The bottom player's legs entangle one of the top player's legs so it cannot be freed to pass; the bottom player gets onto the hip and takes an underhook (arm under the opponent's arm on the trapped-leg side) with the head connected to the body, which stops the crossface flattening them and enables the dogfight, back take or wrestle-up. The top player's goals are the reverse: kill the underhook, win the crossface, flatten and free the leg.

secondary_targets.mechanism: The underhook controls the near shoulder; losing it exposes the bottom player to the crossface.
Lockdown variant (niju-garami) figure-fours the leg and drives the foot upward, stretching the hip and limiting passing.

positions.note: Underhook → dogfight → back take / wrestle-up; lockdown → whip-up → electric chair (10th Planet).
Top control: crossface + underhook + sprawl pressure to flatten, then free the leg (knee cut).
Variant working under the opponent's hips, mostly for sweeps.

ibjjf.note: Half guard does not count as an advantage for the top player if it did not originate from a guard pass attempt (5.7.1–5.7.2).

techniques.summary: Trap one leg between yours, get on your side and win the underhook – the whole half-guard game runs on who controls that leg and that arm.
techniques.notes: The brief's 'underhook on the leg' was interpreted as the half-guard underhook combined with the leg trap; if a leg-underhook (arm under the thigh) was meant, see leg_drag / knee_cut.

techniques.name: Hammerlock / chicken wing

primary_target.mechanism: Forced internal rotation and extension: the arm is bent behind the opponent's back and the hand is driven up toward the neck/scapula, placing pressure on the shoulder

secondary_targets.mechanism: Elbow is flexed and used as the lever; a 'twisting hammerlock' adds elbow torque

positions.note: Arm levered behind the back from the top of turtle
Classic standing control/pin from behind
Arm driven up the back

ibjjf.note: Not on the IBJJF prohibited table; in BJJ it usually appears as a kimura/'chicken wing' finish rather than a stand-alone technique

techniques.summary: Arm bent behind the back and hand pushed up toward the neck; the oldest documented armlock, now mostly a wrestling/control idea or kimura variant.
techniques.notes: No BJJ textbook locator; the 1928 NCAA rulebook banned the twisting hammerlock in wrestling, but it is not listed by the IBJJF.

techniques.name: Hand-on-throat strangle (illegal)

primary_target.mechanism: Direct squeezing of the throat with one or both hands, thumb pressure on the windpipe, or covering the nose/mouth; closes the airway rather than the carotids

positions.note: Self-defence context only

ibjjf.note: 6.2.3-I: strangling without the gi with one or both hands around the neck, or thumb pressure on the windpipe, is a severe foul (DQ); 6.2.3-J: blocking the nose/mouth with the hands is a severe foul.

techniques.summary: Bare-hand throat strangle or smother; explicitly a disqualifying foul in IBJJF competition.
techniques.notes: Included so the app can show why hand-on-throat is never an option in sport BJJ.

techniques.name: Head-and-arm control

primary_target.mechanism: One arm encircles the head and neck while the other controls the near arm; the attacker's hip and ribs pin the chest, leaving the opponent flat with the head immobilised

secondary_targets.mechanism: Hip and body weight on the chest
Arm trapped under the attacker's armpit

positions.note: Judo kesa gatame; precursor to arm triangle, paper cutter, americana
Transition hold

ibjjf.note: Legal pin; side control scores no points but can score an advantage/guard-pass points.

techniques.summary: Classic scarf hold: arm around the head, near arm trapped, hips pinning the chest.

sources.locator: Ch. 8 Winning From the Top Position

techniques.name: Helicopter armbar

primary_target.mechanism: Elbow hyperextension: the attacker grips both arms, falls backward with feet on the hips (tomoe-nage), lifts and rotates the opponent over, and lands with the extended arm across the hips

positions.note: Entered from a double-arm grip or double sleeve grip while standing

ibjjf.note: Not a jumping-guard entry, so not covered by 6.2.2 W; slamming the opponent on landing would be a slam (prohibited at all levels)

techniques.summary: A sacrifice-throw armbar: sit back under the opponent with feet on their hips, spin them over and come up in the armlock.
techniques.notes: Only a Wikipedia description was located; no textbook locator.

techniques.name: Hip control in side control

structures: near hip / pelvis (blocked by knee, hand or hip-to-hip pressure)
primary_target.mechanism: Top player lies chest-to-chest across the face-up opponent with hips low and driving forward; the near-side hip is blocked (knee tight to the hip, hand on the hip, or hip-to-hip) while the crossface turns the head and the underhook controls the far shoulder – together denying the bridge and the hip escape (shrimp).

secondary_targets.mechanism: Crossface turns the head so the spine follows.
Underhook pins the far shoulder.

positions.note: Advance to knee-on-belly or mount when the bottom player reacts; bottom player's priority is to re-entangle a leg (half guard).
Rotational variant that switches hip control for head/shoulder control.

ibjjf.note: Side control scores no points itself; passing to it scores 3 (4.3).

techniques.summary: Chest down, hips heavy, near hip blocked, head crossfaced – side control works by taking away the bridge and the shrimp.
techniques.notes: Textbook locators not verified.

techniques.name: Inside heel hook
aliases: Inside heel hook from the saddle

structures: posterolateral corner: LCL, popliteus tendon, popliteofibular ligament, fabellofibular & arcuate ligaments, biceps femoris tendon
primary_target.mechanism: Attacker's body is on the inside of the leg line (inside sankaku / saddle); the heel is trapped against the attacker's side and rotated toward the opponent's midline while the knees pinch the femur. With the femur fixed, the tibia is driven into maximal EXTERNAL rotation; the foot ends dorsiflexed and everted. Because the thick deltoid ligament limits eversion, the ankle absorbs almost nothing and the full torque reaches the knee quickly.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Eversion is resisted by the deltoid; it tends to avulse bone rather than tear (Piekarski).
Attacker's inside leg wedges across the hip line so the opponent cannot turn to follow the rotation.

positions.note: Inside sankaku / 411 / honey hole – the signature and strongest finishing position (Kesting & Biernacki position 7; Digitsu).
Closed-circuit 50/50 gives the 'reverse heel hook' to both players; the 80/20 variant hides your own inside knee.
Cross ashi (topside ashi): leg switched across the body gives the reverse heel hook (cheat sheet position 2).
Backside 50/50 – see separate entry.

ibjjf.note: Illegal in gi at every belt and in all Master divisions; legal only Adult brown/black no-gi (table row 17). The saddle also involves reaping configurations illegal in gi (row 19).

techniques.summary: The most feared leg lock: from the saddle, trap the heel against your ribs and turn toward the opponent's knee; the torque isolates at the knee and ligaments can fail before pain registers.
techniques.notes: Most BJJ blogs label the inside heel hook 'internal rotation' and credit it with ACL/MCL tears; the orthopaedic review assigns it external tibial rotation (posterolateral corner first) and assigns the ACL/MCL pattern to the outside hook. The eversion/deltoid explanation (Reed; Piekarski) is consistent with the review. 'Inverted/reverse heel hook' is the same mechanism entered with the foot in the opposite armpit.

techniques.name: Japanese necktie

primary_target.mechanism: From a failed D'Arce the arm goes over the neck with the hand on the far shoulder, the other hand locks the grip; the attacker drops to the hip and folds the head down, compressing the carotids between forearm and the opponent's trapped shoulder while flexing the neck

secondary_targets.mechanism: Forward flexion of the head (crank component)

positions.note: Follow-up when the D'Arce stalls
Lachlan Giles demonstrates it from top half guard
Against a turtled opponent

ibjjf.note: Choke with spinal lock (row 2): legal from 16/white, illegal 4-15; widely described as a grey area that depends on the referee.

techniques.summary: D'Arce cousin finished by folding the opponent's head down over your own forearm; a hybrid choke/crank.

sources.locator: Eddie Bravo quoted calling it a grey area

techniques.name: Kimura

structures: posterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament / posterior capsule
primary_target.mechanism: Forced internal (medial) rotation plus extension of the humerus with the elbow flexed ~90 deg, driving the hand up behind the back; a figure-four grip (one hand on the wrist, the other through and gripping your own wrist) uses the forearm as a lever

secondary_targets.mechanism: If the elbow is allowed to open, torque is transmitted to the elbow (double wristlock origin)
The wrist grip can bend the wrist as a finishing adjunct

positions.note: Far-arm kimura; most commonly taught; circle to north-south to finish
Kesting: strongest finishing position; opponent turned on side, arm driven behind the back in a triangle-shaped motion
Sit up, trap the posting arm with the figure-four, fall to the side and swing the arm behind the back; doubles as a sweep
Attack the far arm when the opponent frames on your face or reaches for the back
Kimura grip from half guard bottom feeds sweeps, back takes and the finish
Topside kimura control vs turtle; roll the opponent over to finish
Kimura control from the back (especially no-gi)
When the opponent turns or frames
Standing kimuras; classic counter to a single-leg takedown (kimura grip on the attacker's wrist)

ibjjf.note: Not on the prohibited table; legal in all divisions

techniques.summary: Figure-four bent-arm shoulder lock that rotates the arm inward and up behind the back; Masahiko Kimura used it to beat Helio Gracie in 1951.

sources.locator: posterior-band IGHL elongation at 90 deg abduction + internal rotation

techniques.notes: Anatomical loading: internal rotation tensions the posterior capsule/posterior IGHL and the external rotators; the frequently quoted 'subscapularis' target is actually the muscle being shortened, not stretched.

techniques.name: Kimura grip as a control position

primary_target.mechanism: The figure-four kimura grip is held as a 'giant handle': it immobilises the arm, threatens the shoulder lock, and is used to sweep, pass, take the back, or transition between kimura positions (side control, north-south, near-side, T-kimura, back)

secondary_targets.mechanism: Latent kimura threat

positions.note: Kimura grip to sweep/back take; 'kimura trap' systems (Avellan)
Kimura sweep when the lock is defended
Kimura-based guard passing and pinning
Topside kimura control vs turtle to roll the opponent
Kimura control from the back
Kimura grip on a single-leg attempt

techniques.summary: Treat the kimura grip as a position, not just a finish: it controls the arm and moves the opponent between side, north-south, back and sweeps.

techniques.name: Knee cut pass

structures: opponent's bottom thigh (sliced by the passer's shin/knee)
primary_target.mechanism: The passer drops the lead knee across the opponent's bottom thigh and slices it diagonally toward the mat and far hip, flattening the bottom leg and blocking the hip escape; the trailing leg posts wide and windshield-wipes free of hooks; upper body wins the underhook (or crossface/collar) first so the back is not exposed, driving chest-to-shoulder until the knee clears into side control.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Knee pins the hip line so the bottom player cannot shrimp or turn in.

structures: near shoulder / arm (underhook or sleeve control)
secondary_targets.mechanism: Without the underhook the knee cut gives up the back (Gracie Barra).

positions.note: Classic pass once the underhook is won; Xande Ribeiro's half-guard pass ends with underhook + head control.
From headquarters / combat base vs DLR, RDLR, knee shield; block the outside knee first against the shield.
Counter: Estima lock is available if a foot pushes on the hip during the knee cut.

techniques.summary: Slice your knee diagonally across their thigh to the mat with the underhook secured – pins the hip and bottom leg and lands in side control.
techniques.notes: Jiu-Jitsu University's guard-passing chapter is cited without page numbers.

techniques.name: Knee on belly

structures: pelvis and hips (shin across the hip line)
primary_target.mechanism: From side control the top player rises and places the knee/shin across the opponent's abdomen or chest with the other leg posted wide for balance; body weight through the knee compresses the torso (pain, compressive asphyxia) and the shin across the hips blocks turning, while the position stays mobile enough to switch to mount or back.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Shin and posted foot pin the hip line; collar/hip grips hold the opponent flat.
High placement compresses the ribs.

positions.note: Scores 2 points when stabilised 3 s with the knee on the belly/chest and the other foot free (IBJJF 4.4); common follow-up: armbar when the bottom player pushes; calf slicer from a knee ride on the foot.

ibjjf.note: 2 points (Article 4.4).

techniques.summary: Knee across the belly, foot posted, weight down: a mobile pin that hurts, blocks the hips and baits the armbar.

techniques.name: Knee on belly

primary_target.mechanism: Top player places the knee or shin on the opponent's belly, chest or ribs with the other foot posted; body weight drives through the knee, restricting breathing and movement while the attacker stays mobile

secondary_targets.mechanism: Knee can ride up onto the chest

positions.note: The position itself; transitions from side control
Entry

ibjjf.note: Legal; Art. 4.3: 2 points when the knee/shin closest to the hip is on the belly, chest or ribs, other knee off the ground, held 3 s with the opponent on back or side.

techniques.summary: Knee driven into the belly with the other foot posted: a mobile 2-point pin that drains the opponent and opens collar chokes.

techniques.name: Knee reap (reaping position / inside ashi)

primary_target.mechanism: IBJJF definition: the attacker's thigh goes behind the opponent's leg, the calf passes over the body above the knee with the foot beyond the vertical midline, pressing the knee from outside-in while the attacked foot is trapped (between hip and armpit, by a grip, or by being weight-bearing). With the foot fixed the knee cannot rotate to follow a twist, so any rotation (heel hook, or even a bad spin-out) is isolated at the knee – which is why the IBJJF bans it outside Adult brown/black no-gi.

secondary_targets.mechanism: The reap destroys leg alignment and base; opponent cannot stand until untangled (Kesting & Biernacki).

positions.note: Bring the outside leg over the trapped leg and weave it into the other leg (cheat sheet position 6).
The saddle's inside leg across the hip line is itself a reaping configuration in gi rules (Digitsu).
Turning inside from 50/50 while the opponent stands on the guard foot counts as a trapped-foot reap (rulebook p. 33).

ibjjf.note: Row 19 + definition p. 32: illegal in all gi and Master divisions; legal only Adult brown/black no-gi. Crossing the midline, or any reap while either athlete has a submission hold, is a severe foul (DQ). A scoop grip on the free leg is legal because the leg can still rotate (Ryan).

techniques.summary: The leg configuration that makes heel hooks devastating: your leg across their hip line with their foot trapped means the knee alone must absorb any rotation – illegal in gi at every belt.
techniques.notes: The IBJJF rulebook gives no explicit medical rationale; the 'knee cannot rotate with the foot trapped' explanation is from Ryan/FloGrappling and Piekarski (DPT) who adds that injury mostly occurs when the defender fights the torque.

techniques.name: Knee shield (half guard)

structures: opponent's hip / lower torso (framed by the shin)
opponent's trapped thigh and knee (hooked by the bottom leg)
primary_target.mechanism: Bottom player in half guard keeps the trapped leg hooked with the bottom leg while the top shin lies diagonally across the opponent's hip/torso (foot on the hip or thigh, knee toward their shoulder); the shin is a frame that manages distance, blocks smash/over-under pressure and the crossface, and lets the bottom player push-pull to win the underhook.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Bottom leg hooks or clamps the thigh so the leg cannot be freed (Z-guard: feet locked, knee pressuring the hip).
Arm frames (crossface block / underhook) complete the barrier.

positions.note: Attacks: push sweep, back-take sweep, triangle, armbar, omoplata, kimura; transitions to butterfly, deep half, full guard. Top player counters by collapsing a low knee, smashing the shin flat and circling, or knee-cutting after blocking the outside knee.

techniques.summary: Half guard with your top shin across their hip as a frame: keeps the passer's weight off, blocks the crossface and sets up sweeps and the underhook.
techniques.notes: Sources differ on whether 'Z-guard' means knee at the hip (Evolve) or shin across the torso (JitsuIQ). Jiu-Jitsu University covers half guard but no page locator was found.

techniques.name: Kneebar

structures: posteromedial capsule and posterior oblique ligament (>50% of hyperextension resistance)
primary_target.mechanism: The leg is trapped between the attacker's thighs with the opponent's kneecap against the attacker's hip and the foot pinned at the chest/armpit; hip extension applies a force vector perpendicular to the knee in an anterior-to-posterior direction, driving the tibiofemoral joint into supraphysiologic hyperextension (normal range only ~5–10°). In practice varus/valgus and torsion are added.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Foot is often hugged in an Achilles-lock grip; pulling the heel adds plantarflexion.
Posture of the trapped hip is controlled by the attacker's legs; Suloev stretch variants load hamstring/hip first.

positions.note: Top player back-steps / spins over the trapped leg when it straightens.
Spinning kneebar when the bottom player bridges or pushes the hips (JitsuIQ).
Rolling kneebar: hook behind the knee left between your legs and roll under (Digitsu/Koepfer, Humphreys).
Extend the trapped leg across the body from 50/50 or the 90/10.
Lateral kneebar: lie flat and extend the trapped leg from inside sankaku (Sweet Science of Fighting position B2).
Isolate the leg during the sweep; also from single-leg X.
Rear ashi ('kneebar in progress'): sitting on the diaphragm facing the legs after a back-step pass (Kesting & Biernacki position 8).

ibjjf.note: Table row 14: illegal for 4–17, white, blue, purple; legal brown/black gi and no-gi.

techniques.summary: An armbar on the leg: pinch the thigh, hug the foot, hips through the kneecap – the knee hyperextends and the posterior capsule and cruciates give way.

sources.locator: B2 lateral kneebar, B3 classic kneebar

techniques.notes: Hasegawa cites Noyes et al. for the hyperextension-restraint ordering; a case of intra-articular patellar dislocation after a kneebar is reported but rare.

techniques.name: Lasso guard (lasso hook)

primary_target.mechanism: With a sleeve grip, the leg spirals outside and around the opponent's arm so the shin lies across the biceps and the foot hooks into the armpit or back; the trapped arm cannot post or grip and the shoulder is pulled down, breaking posture

secondary_targets.mechanism: Same-side sleeve grip is pulled constantly

positions.note: Primary position; attacks: omoplata, triangle, sweeps, bicep slicer, back take
Combined spider-lasso
Lasso + DLR hook

ibjjf.note: Gi only (sleeve-dependent). Bicep slicer finishes from the lasso remain brown-belt-only

techniques.summary: A leg wrapped around the arm with the shin on the biceps: harder to strip than spider guard and a direct door to the omoplata.

techniques.name: Leg drag

structures: opponent's dragged leg (shin/thigh pinned across the passer's hip)
primary_target.mechanism: Grip the ankle or pant cuff and pull the leg across your body to the opposite hip while stepping the hips forward; the dragged thigh is pinned against the passer's hip/thigh and the knee stapled to the mat, the near knee slides tight to the opponent's hip to stop shrimping, the free hand controls the far hip or belt, and the chest drops onto the torso at an angle toward the back. Misdirection: legs go one way, body goes the other.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Far-hip control prevents turning away to turtle or re-guarding; sets up back takes.
Knee stapled to the mat with hand/thigh pressure.

positions.note: The passing position itself; finishes to side control, back take or smash pass.
Standing pass vs open guard / DLR (Mendes brothers modern version; earlier Tererê, Shaolin).
Cross ashi with the leg across the body converts directly into a leg drag (Kesting & Biernacki).

techniques.summary: Drag their leg across your hip, pin the knee, own the far hip and angle toward their back – the pass is really the control after the drag.

techniques.name: Lockdown (half guard)

structures: hip flexors of the trapped side (stretched when the foot is driven up)
primary_target.mechanism: Bottom half guard with a figure-four leg configuration: the outside leg hooks over the trapped leg, the inside leg hooks under it, and the longer leg drives the opponent's foot upward and away, extending their hip, breaking posture and limiting passing; it feeds the whip-up, dogfight, electric chair, calf slicer and banana split.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Stretching the leg back extends the opponent's hip and pulls them flat.

positions.note: 10th Planet half-guard system; limited submissions directly, better sweeps/reversals (Wikipedia).

techniques.summary: Figure-four your legs around their trapped leg and stretch it back – the 10th Planet half guard that launches the electric chair and calf slicer.

techniques.name: Loop choke

primary_target.mechanism: A shallow cross-collar grip is looped over the opponent's head as the head is snapped down; the forearm passes over the neck and the free hand behind the head closes the loop so the collar cuts into both carotids

secondary_targets.mechanism: Head is pushed down and under the looping arm

positions.note: After a sprawl or snap-down
Classic entry when the passer's head is low
Against a passer driving forward
Seated guard loop choke

ibjjf.note: Gi only; legal in all divisions.

techniques.summary: Collar grip looped over the opponent's lowered head; the arm wraps and rolls to tighten the lapel across the carotids.
techniques.notes: Sources are coaching blogs; judo naming is inconsistent.

techniques.name: Marceloplata

primary_target.mechanism: Forced internal rotation of the trapped arm, as in the omoplata, re-secured when the opponent is slipping out of the standard finish (the arm is re-clamped and the shoulder re-torqued from a modified leg/hip configuration)

positions.note: Follow-up when a regular omoplata is almost finished but the opponent is escaping

ibjjf.note: Shoulder lock, not on the prohibited table

techniques.summary: A Marcelo Garcia omoplata follow-up used when the opponent is slipping out of the standard omoplata.
techniques.notes: Only a Grapplearts tag page (video tutorial) was located; written mechanics are not described in text, so the exact leg/grip configuration is unverified.

techniques.name: Mir lock

primary_target.mechanism: Forced internal rotation with the elbow clamped: a figure-four grip on the wrist with the opponent's elbow pinned tightly to the attacker's chest/hip, then the wrist is rotated toward the opponent's back ('paintbrush') so all torque goes to the shoulder

secondary_targets.mechanism: Elbow is trapped and compressed against the chest; some descriptions say it attacks elbow and shoulder together

positions.note: Named for Frank Mir's finish of Pete Williams (UFC 36, 2002); overhook the arm, sit up and lock the figure-four as the opponent pulls away
Digitsu describes it from kesa-gatame / combat base with hip pressure

ibjjf.note: A shoulder lock, not on the prohibited table (it is NOT a wrist lock, so no blue-belt restriction)

techniques.summary: A tight kimura/keylock hybrid with the elbow trapped against your body and the wrist rotated toward the opponent's back.
techniques.notes: Sources conflict: some call it a kimura variant, some an americana variant with elbow/shoulder together. The task brief grouped it with supination wrist locks; the located sources describe a shoulder lock. Origin (Mir vs Williams UFC 36) not verified in the sources retrieved.

techniques.name: Monoplata

primary_target.mechanism: Forced internal rotation/hyper-rotation with the arm trapped: one leg drapes over the opponent's back and hooks the arm near the elbow (arm held above the hips and under the armpit), the attacker's thigh and ribs control the arm and hip pressure drives into the shoulder

positions.note: From 3/4 mount when the opponent turns to take an underhook; separate the arm, lean and swing the leg to trap it
Reaction to the underhook pummel

techniques.name: Wrist lock - flexion (gooseneck)

primary_target.mechanism: Forced palmar flexion of the wrist past its end range: the hand is pushed toward the inner forearm while the forearm/elbow is immobilised (elbow and shoulder must be controlled so the opponent cannot roll the arm out)

positions.note: Against a hand posted on the chest or a collar/lapel grip: cup the triceps, fold the hand with your chest/hands and drive the hips forward
Fold the wrist of a hand pushing on the chest/hip
From a kimura grip: hands control the wrist, biceps the elbow, ribs the shoulder (Kesting)
'Sitting on the shoulder' after an omoplata sweep: belly and hand control the wrist, calf/hamstring clamp the shoulder
Against a gi collar grip the trapped wrist is folded (gi only); rarely finishes standing

ibjjf.note: IBJJF Rules Book v6.1 p. 29 table row 10 'Wrist lock': prohibited for 4-12, 13-15, 16-17 (all ranks) and all white-belt divisions; permitted for adult blue belt and above (gi and no-gi)

techniques.summary: Bend the hand toward the inside of the forearm while the elbow and shoulder are pinned - the 'gooseneck'.
techniques.notes: Legality verified against the rendered IBJJF table (2026-10-11); earlier blog claims of purple/brown thresholds are wrong for the current rules. A wristlock 'from spider guard' was requested but no source describing it was found, so it is omitted.

techniques.name: Wrist lock - hyperextension

primary_target.mechanism: Forced dorsiflexion/hyperextension: the knuckles are driven back toward the forearm, usually by pinning the palm flat and driving weight through the straight arm, or by bending the hand back against a trapped forearm

secondary_targets.mechanism: Often combined with finger extension - illegal if fingers are bent backwards (IBJJF row 24)

positions.note: Against a stiff arm posted on the chest: pin the hand flat to your chest and sit up/drive the hips
Pin a framing hand flat to your shoulder/chest and press
Counter when the opponent grabs your wrist: grab four fingers/hand and turn the hand back (Evolve)

ibjjf.note: Wrist lock row 10: legal from adult blue belt. Bending the fingers backwards (row 24) is prohibited at every level, so the hand must be controlled as a whole

techniques.summary: Pin the palm and drive the knuckles back toward the forearm; weak on its own, strong against a stiff-arm frame.

techniques.name: Wrist lock - rotational (supination / pronation)

primary_target.mechanism: Forced supination or pronation beyond end range: the wrist itself does not rotate, so the twist is transmitted to the distal and proximal radioulnar joints and, with the elbow straightened, to the shoulder; usually combined with flexion (kote-gaeshi) or pronation with the elbow bent (nikyo/sankyo)

secondary_targets.mechanism: Torsion of the forearm bones
With a straight elbow the rotation ends at the shoulder

positions.note: Sankyo-style pronating wristlock from rear mount (Kesting)
Supinating twist on a hand that grips your collar/lapel (gi) or posts on the chest
From the kimura grip, rotate the hand rather than the shoulder
Kote-gaeshi style takedown-wristlock; low percentage in competition because elbow/shoulder are free

ibjjf.note: Wrist lock row 10: legal from adult blue belt; prohibited for all juvenile and white-belt divisions

techniques.summary: Twist the hand into full supination or pronation while the elbow is pinned so the forearm joints, not the wrist, take the torque.

sources.locator: Rotational, supinating and pronating wristlock sections
sankyo from rear mount; kimura-grip finish

techniques.notes: The brief's 'supination/Mir lock' label does not match located sources: the Mir lock is documented as a shoulder lock (see mir_lock).

techniques.name: Z-lock

primary_target.mechanism: The opponent's leg is folded into a Z (hip flexed, knee bent, foot turned) – typically after they bend and turn the leg to defend an inside heel hook. The ankle is trapped to the attacker's body, the knee line pinned, and the attacker rotates the whole body around the bent leg so torque loads the knee and hip rather than the foot.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Rotation with the knee flexed also torques the femur in the acetabulum.
Ankle is only an anchor; pushing on the foot is explicitly NOT the finish.

positions.note: Cross ashi and related entanglements; systematised by Junny Ocasio (Digitsu).
Arises when the opponent turns the knee to kill the inside heel hook; kneebar, toe hold and heel hook stay live.

ibjjf.note: Not named in the rulebook; a 'lock twisting the knee' (row 18): illegal in gi, Adult brown/black no-gi only.

techniques.summary: When the inside-heel-hook defender folds the leg into a Z, trap the ankle and knee line and rotate your whole body – the twist goes into the knee and hip, not the foot.
techniques.notes: Single source; the brief calls it a foot lock but the source describes a knee/hip rotational lock.
